hints: Look at the ring of small dark clusters in Fig. 1.1 - each one is a vascular bundle with two transport tissues, so think about which side of the bundle faces the outside of the stem.
walkthrough:
Picture the stem in cross-section**
You are looking down a young herbaceous stem. Around the edge you have protective and packing tissues, then a ring of vascular bundles, then large parenchyma cells inside, with a hollow pith in the centre.

Place phloem inside each bundle**
In a stem vascular bundle, xylem is on the inside (towards the centre) and phloem is on the outside (towards the epidermis). The phloem often stains more darkly as small cells. Your label line must touch the outer dark region of any one of those ring bundles.
Final answer: Draw a label line to the phloem in one vascular bundle - the outer part of the bundle, on the side towards the outside of the stem.

hints: Start by separating the jobs of the two vascular tissues - xylem mainly moves water and minerals up, so what different group of dissolved substances must phloem carry?
Now think about direction - leaves make food but roots, buds and storage organs need it, so how would you describe movement from where it is made to where it is needed?
walkthrough:
Name what is moved**
Phloem sieve tubes do not carry water for transpiration. They carry the products of photosynthesis - assimilates or photosynthates - mainly sucrose, plus amino acids and other organic nutrients.

Give the source to sink pattern**
This is called translocation. It moves substances from source to sink. Source means where they are made or released, like a photosynthesizing leaf. Sink means where they are needed for respiration and growth or stored, like roots, buds, flowers, fruits and storage organs.
Final answer: Transport / translocation of assimilates such as sucrose, sugars, amino acids from source (areas of synthesis e.g. leaf) to sink (areas of growth, activity or storage).

hints: Look at the very thin dark rim around the whole section in Fig. 1.1 - what single layer of protective tissue always covers the outside of a young stem or leaf?
walkthrough:
Spot the outer boundary**
The outermost line in the photomicrograph is a single layer of closely packed cells with no intercellular spaces. That protective covering in a young herbaceous stem is the epidermis, often with a waxy cuticle outside it to reduce water loss.

hints: To draw tissues in correct proportion you need to measure relative widths under the microscope itself - what small scale can be placed inside the eyepiece to compare sizes?
walkthrough:
Measure inside the microscope**
You cannot use a ruler on the slide. A transparent scale called an eyepiece graticule is inserted into the eyepiece. Its divisions are lined up across the tissues so you can count how many units wide each tissue is and keep the same ratios in your plan diagram.

hints: First list in your head what an animal cell has, then think what extra features a plant cell must show - do not plan to label nucleus, mitochondria or membranes.
Think about shape and strength - what regular outline and extra outer layer gives a plant cell its fixed shape?
Think about the biggest space inside a mature plant cell that stores water and keeps the cell turgid - what is it and what is its surrounding membrane called?
Think about photosynthesis and food storage - what green organelle and what white storage grain are found only in plants?
Finally, think how neighbouring plant cells are directly linked through tiny channels in the walls - what are those connections called?
walkthrough:
Draw a clear plant cell outline**
Draw a regular shape with sharp corners and two lines close together for the wall. Inside, draw a large central vacuole taking up most of the volume, pushing a thin layer of cytoplasm to the edge. This immediately shows a typical mature plant cell.

Add only plant-only details**
You can include a chloroplast with internal membranes and a small starch grain inside it. You can show tiny channels through the wall between adjacent cells. Keep the drawing simple with clean single lines, no shading.

Label correctly to gain marks**
Label with straight label lines: cellulose cell wall, large permanent vacuole, tonoplast for the vacuole membrane, chloroplast, starch grain, plasmodesmata. Do not label nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body or cell surface membrane, as these also occur in animal cells and lose marks.

Final answer: Draw a regular-shaped (e.g. rectangular) plant cell with a cell wall and a large central vacuole. Label only plant-only structures, e.g. cellulose cell wall, large / permanent / central vacuole, tonoplast, plasmodesmata, chloroplast, starch grain / granule.
